fact_sheet.business_description: American Express combines a recognized travel-payments franchise with financial-services activities including IDS [D01]. The core charge-card brand links cardholders, merchants, and a service promise [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Charge-card services: sold to cardholders and merchants; they buy based on a promise to pay and merchant acceptance [D01], [D03].
Financial services: investment/advisory services (IDS) and banking products [D01], [D03], [D06].
economics: Travel payments combine service charges with funds held between receipt and settlement [D01], [D06].
Internal business pretax margins are approximately 14.6% for travel-related services, 19.8% for investment/advisory services, and 17.3% for banking [D06].
Travel-related services ROE was 23.8% in Q2 1994, while bank ROE was 10.03% [D06].
earnings_record: H1 1994 total net income $710M vs $659M in H1 1993 [D03].
competitive_position: Integrated service model; business includes 35.6 million cards and 3.7 million merchant locations as of June 30, 1994 [D03].
Competes with bank-issued payment networks through acceptance, pricing, and benefits [D06].
Moat evidence: a recognizable name, but not sufficient evidence of an economic franchise without repeat purchasing and customer loyalty [D01].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Bank tier-1 capital 6.6% and total capital 13.0% as of mid-1994 [D06].
management_and_capital_allocation: Harvey Golub's leadership involves moving away from an unfocused financial conglomerate toward payments and financial services [D01], [D03].
Management record: currently focused on restructuring [D03], [D05].

yields_pct.basis: Trailing earnings yield based on $26.50 share price and FY1993 adjusted continuing EPS of $2.30 [D04]. Dividend yield annualizes the $0.225 quarterly payment [D04]. US 10-year Treasury as of August 1, 1994 [D04].

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Competitive card networks and merchant resistance to fees [D05], [D06].
Difficulty of reversing an unfocused conglomerate strategy [D05].
deal_terms_if_any: 1991 preferred investment: $300M, 8.85% coupon, convertible to common [D02], [D04].
recent_events: July 25, 1994: Q2 results released showing revenue net of interest of $3,508M [D03].
berkshire_context: Berkshire has pre-existing preferred or related common exposure [D07], [D08].
document_conflicts: Reported 1993 book value varies: $16.81 (consolidated) vs $11.81 (post-distribution pro-forma) [D02].
missing_data: Complete current cash-flow and tangible-capital reconciliation [D03].
Dated external payment/bank peer P/E/P/B/TBV grid [D06].
Current consolidated balance sheet and exact August 1 market price [D02], [D04].

understandable.evidence: The company operates a core, recognizable payment-processing and financial services franchise that provides essential utility to merchants and cardholders [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: The business operates a massive network with 35.6 million cards and 3.7 million merchant locations, providing a defensible scale and service-based moat [D03].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Despite historical volatility, the core franchise shows strong recovery in earnings with 1993 net income of $1.478 billion and improved H1 1994 performance [D02], [D03].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: Travel-related services demonstrate high profitability with 23.8% ROE, and bank capital ratios meet regulatory requirements [D06].

capital_intensity.evidence: The payment business acts as a financial utility requiring reasonable capital levels, and the company is successfully refining its capital allocation [D01], [D06].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Harvey Golub is executing a clear, rational strategy to divest non-core assets and focus on the primary payments franchise [D01], [D03].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: With a market capitalization of $13.12 billion, the company is sufficiently large to impact Berkshire's portfolio [D04].

price_screen.evidence: The earnings yield of 8.68% is comfortably above the long bond yield of 7.13%, providing a reasonable margin of safety [D04].

conflicts_resolved: Book value: Relied on post-distribution pro-forma value of $11.81 as it better reflects the ongoing, refocused core business [D02].
gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: A resilient payment network franchise successfully refocusing its capital and operations.

gate2.why_available: The market is wary of American Express due to historical earnings volatility and the challenges of reversing a previous period of unfocused, conglomerate-style management [D02], [D05]. Investors under-rate the enduring strength of the core payments franchise, which Harvey Golub is successfully sharpening through divestitures and a renewed focus on the primary business [D01], [D03]. We expect value to manifest as this operational refocusing continues to improve efficiency and demonstrate the resilience of the company's powerful network [D03].
evidence: Golub is actively divesting non-core assets to focus on the payments franchise [D01], [D03].
The core network maintains 35.6 million cards and 3.7 million merchant locations [D03].
Net income has recovered to $1.478 billion in 1993 with strong H1 1994 performance [D02], [D03].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market fears that competitive pressure from bank-issued cards and merchant resistance to fees, combined with the difficulty of organizational restructuring, permanently impairs the franchise's earnings power [D05], [D06].
what_must_be_true: The core payment network continues to hold its value proposition for both merchants and cardholders.
Management maintains discipline in shedding unrelated businesses and controlling costs.
Consumer credit losses remain within manageable, normalized bounds.

key_assumptions: Maintenance of competitive moat in payments [D01]

gate3.price_vs_value: 88% of low-end; margin of safety is tight given the transition status
gate3.alternatives: Long bonds at 7.13% [D04]; American Express offers superior potential for earnings growth through efficiency gains compared to fixed-income returns
gate3.downside_case: Operational restructuring fails or credit losses spike, risking stagnation; not permanent loss as assets remain valuable
flagged_assumptions: Normalization of owner earnings assumed to match 1993 EPS as no precise capital expenditure data is in pack [D02]

gate4.role_description: We are a permanent passive holder; our edge is our patience and our willingness to hold capital through operational cycles while the business compounds [D01], [D03].
value_realisation_path: Realisation of value occurs as Harvey Golub successfully sheds non-core assets, improves efficiency, and the market recognizes the enduring resilience of the core payments franchise [D01], [D03].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: In the 1980-1999 era, we seek consumer franchises at fair prices; we act as a long-term owner of the business's earnings power rather than a short-term trader or active restructurer.

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of pricing power due to successful merchant revolts against fee structures
Credit loss ratios exceeding historical norms due to a systemic economic downturn
Management abandons the focus on the core payments franchise in favor of conglomerate expansion
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must maintain sufficient liquidity to manage potential insurance float obligations and adhere to regulatory capital requirements [D06].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Long-term Treasury bonds yielding 7.13% [D04]; adding to current holdings such as Coca-Cola which offer more predictable earnings growth.
gate5.decider_reason: American Express is a well-understood consumer franchise that fits squarely within the investment criteria for the current era.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The primary risk is a failure to successfully execute the operational turnaround, resulting in stagnation of earnings power rather than a permanent loss of capital.

valuation.downside_case: Operational restructuring fails or credit losses spike, leading to stagnant earnings without permanent capital loss.

drivers.driver: The company sells at an earnings yield of 8.68% against a long bond yield of 7.13%, providing a margin of safety for a business in transition [D04].
The core franchise remains powerful, anchored by a network of 35.6 million cards and 3.7 million merchant locations that provide essential utility [D03].
Harvey Golub is taking the right steps to sharpen the focus of the business by divesting non-core assets and prioritizing the payments franchise [D01], [D03].
The travel-related services business has demonstrated strong profitability with an ROE of 23.8%, showing the underlying potential of the core operations [D06].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of pricing power due to successful merchant revolts against fee structures
Credit loss ratios exceeding historical norms due to a systemic economic downturn
Management abandons the focus on the core payments franchise in favor of conglomerate expansion
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A failure to execute the operational turnaround that results in a permanent impairment of the franchise's competitive position or a sustained departure from the focus on core payment services.
final.memo:
We understand American Express well; it is a core, recognizable financial utility that connects cardholders and merchants through a clear, essential service promise [D01]. While the company lost its way in past years by wandering into unrelated fields, it remains a franchise of significant scale with 35.6 million cards and 3.7 million merchant locations in place as of mid-1994 [D03].

Harvey Golub is now acting like the owner we want to see, methodically shedding non-core assets to restore the business to its primary mission [D01], [D03]. When we look at the travel-related services segment, we see a business that can generate returns on equity as high as 23.8%, which confirms the strength of the underlying economic engine [D06].

The market has been wary, fearing that competitive pressures and the difficulty of organizational restructuring will permanently diminish earnings power [D05], [D06]. However, the 1993 net income of $1.478 billion and the continued recovery observed in the first half of 1994 suggest the franchise has much more durability than current skeptics believe [D02], [D03].

At a price of $26.50, we are paying an earnings yield of 8.68%, which compares favorably to the 7.13% available from long-term Treasury bonds [D04]. While the margin of safety is tighter than we might prefer, we are confident that a patient approach will be rewarded as the company realizes its true earnings potential [D03], [D04].

We are sizing this at 10% of our equity portfolio, as the risk is primarily one of operational execution rather than permanent loss of capital [D05]. We will hold this position indefinitely, waiting for the market to eventually recognize the strength of the refined franchise [D01], [D03].
